'''''Mathematics and the Imagination''''' is a book written by [[Edward Kasner]] and [[James R. Newman]] and illustrated by [[Rufus Isaacs (game theorist)|Rufus Isaacs]], who provided 169 figures. It was published in New York by [[Simon & Schuster]] in 1940.  It rapidly became a best-seller and received several glowing reviews. This book introduced the term [[googol]] for 10<sup>100</sup>, and [[googolplex]] for 10<sup>googol</sup>. It includes nine chapters, an annotated bibliography of 45 titles, and an index in its 380 pages.

==Reception==
[[I. Bernard Cohen]] described it as "the best account of modern mathematics... written in a graceful style, combining clarity of exposition with good humor." Cohen believed it was suitable for both mathematicians and non-mathematicians alike.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cohen |first=I. Bernard |date=June 1942 |title=Reviewed Works: ''A Mathematician's Apology'' by G. H. Hardy; ''Mathematics and the Imagination'' by Edward Kasner, James Newman |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/330724 |journal=[[Isis (journal)|Isis]] |volume=33 |issue=6 |pages=723-5}}</ref> According to T. A. Ryan the book "is not as superficial as one might expect a book at the popular level to be. For instance, the description of the invention of the term ''googol'' ... is a very serious attempt to show how misused is the term ''infinite'' when applied to large and finite numbers."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ryan |first=T. A. |date=December 1940 |title=Reviewed Work: ''Mathematics and the Imagination'' by Edward Kasner, James Newman, Rufus Isaacs |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2302495 |journal=[[The American Mathematical Monthly]] |volume=47 |issue=10 |pages=700-1}}</ref> [[G. Waldo Dunnington]] could note the book had become a [[best-seller]] by 1941, writing, "Apparently it has succeeded in communicating to the layman something of the pleasure experienced by the creative mathematician in difficult problem solving."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dunnington |first=G. Waldo |date=January 1941 |title=Reviewed Work: ''Mathematics and the Imagination'' by Edward Kasner, James Newman |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3028140 |journal=National Mathematics Magazine |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=212-3}}</ref>

==Contents==
'''Chapter I''' ("New Names for Old") explains the significance of the concept of the [[Function (mathematics)|function]], the notions of [[Ring (mathematics)|rings]] and [[Group (mathematics)|groups]] from [[abstract algebra]], the [[Problem of Apollonius]], radicals, and the [[Abel–Ruffini theorem]], or impossibility of solving polynomial equations of the fifth or higher degree by radicals.

'''Chapter II''' ("Beyond Googol") treats the size or [[cardinality]] of a set,  [[Infinite set|infinite sets]], the differences between [[Countable set|countable]] and [[Uncountable set|uncountable sets]], Cantor's theory of [[Transfinite number|transfinite numbers]],  and the [[cardinality of the continuum]], or the set of [[Real number|real numbers]] <math>\mathbb{R}</math>.

'''Chapter III''' ("<math>\pi</math>, <math>i</math>, <math>e</math> (Pie)") goes over [[Algebraic number|algebraic]] and [[Transcendental number|transcendental numbers]], the impossibility of [[doubling the cube]] or [[Angle trisection|trisecting an angle]] by a [[Straightedge and compass construction|straightedge and compass]], the histories of [[E (mathematical constant)|Euler's number]] <math>e</math> and <math>\pi</math> ([[pi]]), the exponential function <math>y = e^x</math>, the [[imaginary unit]] <math>i</math>, the [[complex plane]], the geometric interpretation of multiplication by <math>i</math> as rotating by 90° counterclockwise, and [[Euler's identity]] <math>e^{i \pi} + 1 = 0</math>.

'''Chapter IV''' ("Assorted Geometries—Plane and Fancy") examines [[Euclid's fifth postulate]], [[non-Euclidean geometry]], and [[four-dimensional space]].

'''Chapter V''' ("Pastimes of Past and Present Times") discusses various mathematical games or puzzles such as the [[Tower of Hanoi]] and the [[magic square]]; the [[decimal]] and [[Binary number|binary system]]s; and [[Fermat's Last Theorem]].

'''Chapter VI''' ("Paradox Lost and Paradox Regained") explores a number of paradoxes or fallacies in mathematics, such as the [[Banach–Tarski paradox]] in geometry and [[Russell's paradox]] in set theory.

'''Chapter VII''' ("Chance and Chanceablity") is about various topics in [[probability]] and [[statistics]], such as [[Buffon's needle problem]] and the [[binomial theorem]].

'''Chapter VIII''' ("Rubber-sheet Geometry") concerns concepts in [[topology]], such as the [[Jordan curve theorem]], the [[Euler characteristic]]s, and the [[Four color theorem|four-color map theorem]].

'''Chapter IX''' ("Change and Changeability") elucidates the [[calculus]], [[History of calculus|its history]], and applications.
